title: Idempotence and repeat runs
summary: A good playbook changes nothing on the second run. See how raw shell tasks report change every time and hide real drift.

inputs.label: Tasks that use shell or command
Those tasks have creates or changed_when

nodes.label: Real drift
nodes.sub: noisy>0 ? "hidden among the noise" : "visible at once"

readouts.label: Tasks that use shell or command
Tasks reporting change on a repeat run
Changed task results across all hosts

verdicts.text: Every run reports changes, so a real change is lost among the noise and you cannot trust check mode. Use modules, or add creates and changed_when.
The shell tasks are guarded, so a repeat run reports no change unless something really drifted.
All tasks use idempotent modules, so a clean second run is the proof.

tries: Use 60 percent shell tasks with no guards.
Add guards.
Remember a second run showing zero changes is the test.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: Every run reports changes, so a real change is lost among the noise and you cannot trust check mode.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: All tasks use idempotent modules, so a clean second run is the proof.

title: Forks and serial rollouts
summary: Forks set how many hosts run at once, serial sets how many are changed per batch. See runtime against how many hosts a bad change hits before you stop.

inputs.label: Serial batch size (0 for all at once)

readouts.label: Hosts hit before a failure stops the run

verdicts.text: A bad change reaches a quarter or more of the fleet before anything can stop it. Use serial with a small first batch and max_fail_percentage.
Over an hour. Raise forks, or run in waves.
Small batches limit damage and the run finishes in reasonable time.

tries: Run 300 hosts at once.
Set serial to 10. The blast radius drops.
Raise forks to cut the runtime.

chart.y: (ceil(hosts / (serial == 0 ? hosts : min(serial, hosts))) * ceil((serial == 0 ? hosts : min(serial, hosts)) / min(forks, (serial == 0 ? hosts : min(serial, hosts)))) * tasks * secs) / 60
chart.title: Runtime against forks

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: A bad change reaches a quarter or more of the fleet before anything can stop it.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: Small batches limit damage and the run finishes in reasonable time.

title: Variable precedence
summary: The same variable can be set in several places. See which one wins as you switch layers on and off.

inputs.label: Extra vars on the command line (value 4)

verdicts.text: Extra vars beat everything, which is easy to forget. Use them for one-off overrides only.
A different layer won than you expected. Role defaults are the lowest, so anything else overrides them.
The winning layer matches your expectation.

tries: Turn on all layers and watch extra vars win.
Remove extra vars. Play vars win.
Set your expected value to 1 while group_vars is on.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: A different layer won than you expected.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: The winning layer matches your expectation.

title: Dynamic inventory cache
summary: A cached inventory is fast but can list machines that no longer exist. See how many stale hosts a cache lets through as the fleet churns.

inputs.label: Refresh the cache before every run

nodes.label: Cached inventory
nodes.sub: refresh ? 'fresh each run' : 'up to ' + ttl + ' min old'

readouts.label: Share of the list that is stale

verdicts.text: A tenth or more of the inventory is wrong. Runs fail on hosts that are gone and skip new ones, so new instances stay unconfigured.
Some stale entries. Expect unreachable host errors.
The list matches the cloud.

tries: Set a 4 hour cache with heavy churn.
Refresh before every run.
Shorten the cache lifetime.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: A tenth or more of the inventory is wrong.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: The list matches the cloud.

title: Pipeline speed
summary: Split tests into shards and cache dependencies. See where adding shards stops paying because of fixed overhead.

verdicts.text: Each shard spends more time on setup than on tests. More shards now cost money and save almost no time.
Slow feedback. Cache dependencies and add shards while the speed-up is still large.
Fast feedback at a sensible cost.

tries: Raise shards to 20.
Turn the cache on and off.
Compare machine minutes with wall time.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: Slow feedback.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: Fast feedback at a sensible cost.

title: Canary exposure
summary: A canary sends a slice of traffic to the new version first. See how many users a bad release reaches before you stop it.

readouts.label: Requests failed by the bad version
If it had gone to everyone for the same time

verdicts.text: Even a canary fails a lot of requests if it is large and the check is slow. Start small and roll back automatically.
Contained, but not small. A smaller slice or a faster check would cut it.
A small slice and a quick check keep the damage small.

tries: Use a 50 percent canary with a 30 minute bake.
Shrink the canary to 1 percent.
Turn on automatic rollback.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: Even a canary fails a lot of requests if it is large and the check is slow.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: A small slice and a quick check keep the damage small.

title: Flaky tests and red pipelines
summary: A small flake rate per test adds up across a big suite. See how often a correct change fails, and what retries do.

inputs.label: Automatic retries of the whole run

readouts.label: Runs that fail with no real bug

verdicts.text: One run in five fails for no reason, so people stop trusting red builds and start ignoring real failures. Quarantine and fix flaky tests.
Enough false failures that people rerun by habit. Retries hide it but cost time.
Failures mean something.

tries: Use 2000 tests with 0.1 percent flake.
Add retries and see the false failures fall but time rise.
Lower the flake rate and watch the effect compound.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: One run in five fails for no reason, so people stop trusting red builds and start ignoring real failures.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: Failures mean something.

title: Promotion lead time
summary: A change moves through environments with soak times and approvals. See how waiting dominates lead time and pushes people toward bigger batches.

readouts.label: Changes per week one pipeline can ship in series

verdicts.text: Several days to ship a change. People batch work to avoid the wait, which makes every release bigger and riskier.
Most of the time is waiting, not work. Automate the approvals you can and shorten soak times with good checks.
A short, mostly automated path.

tries: Add 3 manual approvals of 24 hours.
Remove approvals and shorten soak.
Notice that active time is tiny compared with waiting.

chart.y: stages * work / 60 + stages * soak + gates * appr
chart.title: Lead time against approvals

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: Several days to ship a change.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: A short, mostly automated path.

title: Skill context budget
summary: Descriptions of installed skills sit in context all the time and bodies load only when used. See how many tokens that costs and how much room is left for the task.

verdicts.text: Skills take a fifth of the window before the task has started. Cut descriptions, split big bodies into reference files, and remove skills you do not use.
Either many descriptions or very large bodies. Move detail into files that load only when needed.
Descriptions are cheap and bodies load on demand, which is the point of progressive disclosure.

tries: Install 200 skills with long descriptions.
Shrink each body, moving detail to reference files.
Use more skills in one task and see the load grow.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: Skills take a fifth of the window before the task has started.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: Descriptions are cheap and bodies load on demand, which is the point of progressive disclosure.

title: Trigger evaluation
summary: Test prompts that should trigger a skill and prompts that should not. See precision and recall from your counts.

inputs.label: Prompts that should not trigger it

verdicts.text: The skill often fails to trigger when needed. Make the description say what the user will ask for, in their words.
It triggers on unrelated prompts. Narrow the description and say when not to use it.
It triggers when it should and mostly stays quiet otherwise.

tries: Lower the triggered count of positive prompts.
Raise false triggers.
Find the point where both are high.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: The skill often fails to trigger when needed.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: It triggers when it should and mostly stays quiet otherwise.

title: Scripts versus model steps
summary: Every step a model must get right multiplies the chance of error. See what moving steps into scripts does to end-to-end reliability.

inputs.label: Chance a model step is right
Chance a script step is right

readouts.label: Chance the whole workflow is right
With every step done by the model

verdicts.text: Errors compound across steps. Move the mechanical, checkable steps into scripts and keep the model for judgement.
Better, but one run in ten still fails.
Scripts carry the deterministic steps, so most runs finish right.

tries: Use 20 steps at 95 percent with no scripts.
Move 15 steps to scripts.
Raise model accuracy and see how little it helps over a long chain.

chart.y: 100 * pow(pm/100, steps - min(scripted, steps)) * pow(ps/100, min(scripted, steps))
chart.title: Reliability against scripted steps

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: Errors compound across steps.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: Scripts carry the deterministic steps, so most runs finish right.

title: Skill supply chain risk
summary: Skills can run scripts and tell the model what to do. See how unreviewed skills from unknown sources raise the number of risky ones.

inputs.label: From sources you do not know

readouts.label: Skills that can change without you knowing

verdicts.text: Many unreviewed skills can run code and reach the network. Review before installing, pin versions, and block outbound network where you can.
Several skills have not been read by anyone you trust.
Unpinned skills can change after you reviewed them.
Most skills are known and reviewed.

tries: Install many skills from unknown sources with network access.
Review them and pin versions.
Turn off network access for scripts.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: Many unreviewed skills can run code and reach the network.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: Most skills are known and reviewed.

title: Disaster recovery strategies
summary: Four common strategies trade cost against recovery time and data loss. Pick one and compare it with what the business needs.

inputs.label: Business can accept data loss of

nodes.label: Business need
nodes.sub: needrto + ' min down, ' + needrpo + ' min loss'

verdicts.text: Too slow to recover and too much data lost for this need. Choose a stronger strategy.
Recovery takes longer than the business can accept.
More data would be lost than the business can accept.
It meets the need, and it costs a lot. Check that the need justifies it.
It meets the need at a modest cost. Test the recovery to prove it.

tries: Pick backup and restore with a 30 minute need.
Pick warm standby.
Lower the accepted loss to zero.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: Too slow to recover and too much data lost for this need.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: It meets the need at a modest cost.

title: Commitment break-even
summary: A commitment is cheaper per hour but paid whether you use it or not. See where it beats on-demand pricing.

inputs.label: Share of the time the resource runs

verdicts.text: Below the break-even you pay for capacity you do not use. On-demand is cheaper.
Close to the break-even. A small drop in usage turns the saving into a loss.
Steady usage well above the break-even makes the commitment worth it.

tries: Set usage to 40 percent with a 40 percent discount.
Raise the discount.
Commit only to the steady base load.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: Below the break-even you pay for capacity you do not use.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: Steady usage well above the break-even makes the commitment worth it.

title: CDN cache hit ratio
summary: A CDN answers from the edge when it has the object. See how the hit ratio changes origin load and average latency.

inputs.label: A full cache purge just happened

verdicts.text: The origin takes thousands of requests per second. A purge or a low hit ratio can overwhelm it. Warm the cache and shield the origin.
After a purge the cache is cold and the origin takes the load until it refills.
A low hit ratio. Check cache headers, query strings and cookies that split the cache.
The edge absorbs most requests.

tries: Drop the hit ratio to 50 percent.
Purge the cache.
Raise hit ratio and see the origin load fall.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: The origin takes thousands of requests per second.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: The edge absorbs most requests.

title: Serverless cold starts
summary: A burst of requests needs more instances than are warm. See how many requests pay the cold start and what provisioned concurrency does.

inputs.label: Requests per second in the burst

readouts.label: Requests that hit a cold start

verdicts.text: Most of the burst lands on cold instances, so many users wait for a start. Provision warm capacity for the burst or shrink the start time.
Some requests are slow because there were not enough warm instances.
Provisioned instances cover the burst, so nobody waits for a cold start.

tries: Start with a 400 req/s burst and no provisioned instances.
Add provisioned instances.
Make invocations shorter and see fewer instances needed.

chart.ylabel: Requests that hit a cold start (%)
chart.title: Cold starts against provisioning

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: Most of the burst lands on cold instances, so many users wait for a start.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: Provisioned instances cover the burst, so nobody waits for a cold start.

title: Permission evaluation
summary: Several policies apply to one request. See how allow, deny and boundaries combine to decide the result.

inputs.label: An identity policy allows the action
A resource policy also allows it
The permissions boundary or organisation limit allows it

vars: deny ? "an explicit deny always wins" : (!bound ? "the boundary does not allow it" : (!grant ? "nothing allows it, so it is denied by default" : "an allow applies and nothing blocks it"))

verdicts.text: An explicit deny beats every allow, so the request is denied however many policies allow it.
A boundary or organisation limit sets the maximum. An allow outside it does nothing.
Nothing allows the action. Access is denied by default.
At least one allow applies and nothing blocks it.

tries: Turn on allows and add an explicit deny.
Remove the boundary.
Remove all allows.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: Nothing allows the action.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: At least one allow applies and nothing blocks it.

title: Permission creep and reviews
summary: People gain access over time and rarely lose it. See how the gap between granted and used permissions grows between reviews.

inputs.label: Share of unused permissions removed at review

verdicts.text: Granted access is more than twice what is used. Every extra permission widens what a stolen account can do. Review more often and remove unused access.
Reviews leave a lot behind. Base removals on usage data, not on memory.
Frequent reviews keep granted access close to what is needed.

tries: Set 24 months between reviews.
Review every month.
Lower the share removed.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: Granted access is more than twice what is used.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: Frequent reviews keep granted access close to what is needed.

title: Key service load and data key caching
summary: Envelope encryption calls the key service to get data keys. See how caching keys keeps you under the service limit.

inputs.label: Operations served by a cached data key
A traffic spike doubles the load

verdicts.text: The key service throttles you, so decrypts fail or retry and the application slows down. Cache data keys for a short time and reuse them.
Close to the limit. A spike will throttle you.
Cached keys keep calls well under the limit.

tries: Turn off caching at 3000 operations per second.
Cache 90 percent.
Add the spike.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: The key service throttles you, so decrypts fail or retry and the application slows down.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: Cached keys keep calls well under the limit.

title: Credential lifetime and exposure
summary: A leaked credential works until it expires or is revoked. See how short-lived tokens shrink the window compared with a static key.

inputs.label: A static key that never expires

vars: stat ? detect + fix : min(life, detect + fix)

readouts.label: How long a leaked credential works

verdicts.text: The attacker has a day or more to use it. Use short-lived credentials from a role or workload identity instead of static keys.
Several hours of access. Shorten the lifetime and speed up detection.
Expiry closes the window quickly, even if nobody notices the leak.

tries: Use a static key with a day to detect.
Switch to a 1 hour token.
Shorten detection time to see the other lever.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: The attacker has a day or more to use it.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: Expiry closes the window quickly, even if nobody notices the leak.

title: Index or full scan
summary: An index helps when a query picks few rows. See where the cost of an index scan passes a full scan.

inputs.label: Share of rows the query returns
An index exists on the column

verdicts.text: There is no index and the query wants very few rows, so the database reads the whole table to find them. Add an index.
The index exists, but the query returns so many rows that reading the table straight through is cheaper, so the planner ignores the index.
The plan matches the query.

tries: Query 0.1 percent of 5 million rows with no index.
Add the index.
Raise the share to 30 percent.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: There is no index and the query wants very few rows, so the database reads the whole table to find them.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: The plan matches the query.

title: Connection pool sizing
summary: Many app instances each hold a pool. See when the total passes the database limit and how many connections the load really needs.

readouts.label: Share of pooled connections in use

verdicts.text: The pools together hold more connections than the database allows, so new connections are refused when instances scale out. Lower the pool per instance or add a pooler in front.
Even perfectly shared, the load needs more connections than the limit allows. Speed up queries or add replicas.
Most connections sit idle yet still cost memory on the database. Shrink the pools.
The pools fit under the limit and match the load.

tries: Scale instances to 100 with a pool of 20.
Shrink the pool.
Slow the queries down and see the needed connections rise.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: The pools together hold more connections than the database allows, so new connections are refused when instances scale out.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: The pools fit under the limit and match the load.

title: Replication lag and data loss
summary: The primary fails and a replica takes over. See how much committed data is lost with asynchronous replication, and what synchronous costs.

nodes.label: Replica
nodes.sub: sync ? 'always caught up' : fmt(lag, 1) + ' s behind'

readouts.label: Slower commits than without a replica wait

verdicts.text: Thousands of acknowledged transactions vanish at failover. If that is not acceptable, use synchronous replication or a quorum commit.
Some acknowledged writes are lost. Know your lag and decide whether that is acceptable.
No acknowledged write is lost. The price is that every commit waits for the replica.
The replica keeps up.

tries: Fail over with 5 seconds of lag at 1000 writes per second.
Turn on synchronous replication.
Raise the round trip time and watch commit time grow.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: Thousands of acknowledged transactions vanish at failover.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: The replica keeps up.

title: Dead rows and long transactions
summary: Updates leave dead rows that vacuum cleans up. See how one long open transaction stops the cleanup and the table swells.
vars: blocked ? upd * open : min(rows * scale/100, upd)

nodes.label: Vacuum
nodes.sub: blocked ? "held back by open transaction" : "cleans as it goes"

verdicts.text: Half the table is dead rows. Scans read far more than they need and indexes swell. Find and end the long transaction, then vacuum.
An open transaction holds back cleanup. The bloat grows for as long as it stays open.
Vacuum keeps up with the updates.

tries: Open a transaction for 12 hours.
Close it by setting the open time to zero.
Raise the update rate.

chart.y: 100 * (open > 0 ? upd * open : min(rows * scale/100, upd)) / rows
chart.title: Bloat against open transaction time

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: Half the table is dead rows.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: Vacuum keeps up with the updates.

title: Goroutine leaks
summary: A goroutine waiting on a channel that nobody closes lives forever. See how a small leak per request becomes a memory problem.

verdicts.text: Gigabytes are held by goroutines that do nothing. The process grows until it is killed. Give every goroutine a way to stop, usually a context.
A steady climb in goroutine count. It looks like a leak, so watch it before it hurts.
Goroutines stop when their work is cancelled.

tries: Leak 2 percent of requests for a week.
Turn on context cancellation.
Reduce the rate and see the slope.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: Gigabytes are held by goroutines that do nothing.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: Goroutines stop when their work is cancelled.

title: Deadlines and wasted work
summary: A request calls three services in turn. See what happens when the last one is slow, and how passing the context stops wasted downstream work.

inputs.label: The context is passed to every call

nodes.label: Service C
nodes.sub: late ? (prop ? 'cancelled at the deadline' : 'keeps working for nothing') : 'finishes in time'

readouts.label: Work done for a caller who left

verdicts.text: The caller gave up, but service C keeps running a request nobody wants. Under load these pile up. Pass the context so cancellation propagates.
The call is too slow for the deadline, but cancellation stops the wasted work.
Service C is called with less time left than it needs. Fail early instead of starting.
Every call finishes within the deadline.

tries: Make service C take 1200 ms with no context passed.
Pass the context.
Lengthen the deadline.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: The caller gave up, but service C keeps running a request nobody wants.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: Every call finishes within the deadline.

title: Worker pools and backpressure
summary: Producers send work into a buffered channel and workers drain it. See when the buffer fills and what happens next.

verdicts.text: The buffer fills in seconds, and then producers block or you drop work. A bigger buffer only delays the problem. Add workers, slow producers, or shed load.
The buffer fills eventually. Decide now what happens when it does: block, drop or reject.
Workers keep up with the producers.

tries: Send 800 items per second with 8 workers of 20 ms.
Add workers.
Raise the buffer and see how little it changes the outcome.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: The buffer fills in seconds, and then producers block or you drop work.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: Workers keep up with the producers.

title: Graceful shutdown
summary: On deploy the server stops accepting work and waits for requests in flight. See how many requests are cut off for a given grace period.

inputs.label: Share of requests that are long

nodes.label: Server
nodes.sub: 'waits ' + grace + ' s for ' + round(inflight) + ' in flight'

nodes.label: Cut off
nodes.sub: round(cut) + ' per pod, ' + round(total) + ' in all'

verdicts.text: The grace period is shorter than a long request, so those requests are killed mid-flight on every deploy. Set the grace period above your longest request, and check the load balancer drains first.
All requests finish before the process exits, so deploys are invisible to users.

tries: Set the grace period to 1 second with 8 second requests.
Raise it above the long request time.
Raise the share of long requests.

presets.label: Break it
presets.story: The grace period is shorter than a long request, so those requests are killed mid-flight on every deploy.

presets.label: Fix it
presets.story: All requests finish before the process exits, so deploys are invisible to users.
